management.patient_counselling: Report nausea, vomiting, visual disturbance (yellow/green halos), confusion or palpitations.
management.exceptions: Digoxin is often established therapy — do not stop it unilaterally; flag for prescriber dose review and level check.

evidence.normalized_proposition: Dronedarone raises serum digoxin via P-glycoprotein inhibition, risking toxicity.

management_override.prescriber_action: Reduced renal function markedly raises digoxin toxicity risk; withhold and confirm the digoxin dose/level plan before supply.

mechanism: Clarithromycin inhibits P-glycoprotein and suppresses gut flora (Eggerthella lenta) that inactivate digoxin, raising serum digoxin; serious/fatal toxicity has been reported, especially in the elderly and in renal impairment.

management.prescriber_action: Consider an antibiotic without this interaction where clinically appropriate; if clarithromycin is used, monitor the digoxin level and consider a temporary dose reduction.
management.monitoring: Serum digoxin level, renal function and heart rate; watch for toxicity during the course and for a few days after.
management.patient_counselling: Report nausea, vomiting, visual disturbance, confusion or palpitations.
management.exceptions: Short antibiotic course — do not stop established digoxin; manage via antibiotic choice, level check and dose adjustment.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — clarithromycin increases serum digoxin concentrations; monitor for digoxin toxicity>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Clarithromycin raises serum digoxin via P-glycoprotein inhibition and gut-flora suppression, risking toxicity.

management_override.prescriber_action: Reduced renal function markedly raises digoxin toxicity risk; withhold and confirm the digoxin dose/level plan or an alternative antibiotic before supply.

mechanism: Loop and thiazide diuretics can cause hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia, which potentiate digoxin binding at the Na/K-ATPase and precipitate toxicity even at therapeutic serum digoxin levels; diuretic-induced volume/renal changes can also raise digoxin levels.

management.prescriber_action: Use recent/actual serum potassium and magnesium to gauge risk; correct and maintain K+ and Mg2+; consider potassium-sparing strategy or supplementation as clinically appropriate.
management.monitoring: Serum potassium, magnesium, renal function and digoxin level; heart rate/rhythm.
management.patient_counselling: Report palpitations, nausea, visual disturbance, weakness or confusion.
management.exceptions: Documented recent normal potassium and magnesium lowers the concern; this is not automatically high-severity for every digoxin+diuretic pair.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia predispose to digoxin toxicity; monitor and correct electrolytes>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Diuretic-induced hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia potentiates digoxin toxicity.

management_override.prescriber_action: Renal impairment worsens both digoxin accumulation and electrolyte derangement; withhold and confirm recent electrolytes and digoxin level/dose plan before supply.

mechanism: Ivabradine lowers heart rate, and bradycardia is itself a risk factor for torsades de pointes; combined with QT-prolonging or other heart-rate-lowering agents the bradycardia/arrhythmia risk is additive and should be weighed on patient risk (baseline QTc, electrolytes, bradycardia, structural heart disease).

management.prescriber_action: Assess baseline heart rate, QTc, electrolytes and the specific TdP risk of the co-prescribed agent; avoid stacking where the added agent is a known torsades risk.
management.monitoring: Heart rate, ECG/QTc and electrolytes as clinically indicated.
management.patient_counselling: Report palpitations, fainting, dizziness or very slow pulse.
management.exceptions: Distinct from the strong-CYP3A4-inhibitor contraindication rule; here the concern is additive bradycardia/QT, weighed on patient risk factors. NOTE: verapamil and diltiazem must NOT be down-tiered into this additive class — they are contraindicated with ivabradine under EMA/UK labelling (avoid under US labelling) and require handling as a contraindication.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — ivabradine causes bradycardia; use caution with other heart-rate-lowering drugs>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Ivabradine adds bradycardia/QT risk when combined with other QT-prolonging or heart-rate-lowering drugs.

management_override.prescriber_action: Ivabradine is independently contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment; do not supply.

mechanism: Dipyridamole blocks cellular reuptake/deamination of adenosine, potentiating and prolonging its effects (profound bradycardia, AV block, hypotension). This is a procedural/administration interaction — adenosine is given IV during a procedure — not an outpatient co-dispensing hazard.

management.prescriber_action: Notify the team administering adenosine that the patient is on dipyridamole; a substantially lower adenosine dose is used (dipyridamole potentiates the effect). For dipyridamole/adenosine-based pharmacologic stress testing, withhold dipyridamole beforehand per local protocol.
management.monitoring: Continuous ECG, heart rate and blood pressure during and after adenosine administration.
management.patient_counselling: Tell the procedural team about all current medicines, including dipyridamole or aspirin-dipyridamole combinations.
management.exceptions: Not an outpatient dispense-time block; the pharmacist action is to communicate the interaction to the administering/procedural team.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — dipyridamole potentiates the effect of adenosine; a lower adenosine dose may be required>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Dipyridamole potentiates and prolongs adenosine's effects, requiring adenosine dose reduction during administration.

mechanism: Additive hyperkalaemia: RAAS blockade plus aldosterone-receptor antagonism both reduce renal potassium excretion.

management.prescriber_action: If intended (e.g. HFrEF), continue per specialist plan with baseline and follow-up potassium/eGFR against product/guideline thresholds; do not add an MRA if baseline K+ is elevated or eGFR is low. Do not stop established therapy at the pharmacy.
management.monitoring: Serum potassium and eGFR at baseline, ~1 week and ~4 weeks after start or dose change, then periodically.
management.patient_counselling: Report muscle weakness or palpitations; avoid potassium-based salt substitutes.
management.exceptions: A new co-prescription with no HF/resistant-hypertension indication warrants clarification rather than routine monitoring.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — paraphrase: hyperkalaemia risk increased with concomitant ACE inhibitors/ARBs>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Spironolactone combined with an ACE inhibitor or ARB increases the risk of hyperkalaemia.

management_override.prescriber_action: MRA add-on generally not recommended at eGFR <30; clarify intent and current potassium before supply.

mechanism: Additive hyperkalaemia: ACEi/ARB reduce aldosterone while amiloride/triamterene block the distal epithelial sodium channel, each cutting renal potassium excretion.

management.prescriber_action: Confirm the combination is intended; check baseline and follow-up potassium/eGFR; avoid initiating in significant renal impairment or pre-existing hyperkalaemia. Do not stop established therapy at the pharmacy.
management.monitoring: Serum potassium and eGFR at baseline and after start/dose change, then periodically.
management.patient_counselling: Report weakness or palpitations; avoid potassium-based salt substitutes.
management.exceptions: Unlike MRAs, ACEi/ARB + amiloride/triamterene is less often guideline-directed; an unexplained pairing warrants clarification.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — paraphrase: hyperkalaemia risk with concomitant ACE inhibitors>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Amiloride/triamterene with an ACE inhibitor or ARB increases the risk of hyperkalaemia.

management_override.prescriber_action: Potassium-sparing diuretic generally avoided at eGFR <30 with RAAS blockade; clarify before supply.

mechanism: Additive hyperkalaemia: exogenous potassium load on top of reduced RAAS-mediated potassium excretion.

management.prescriber_action: For UNprescribed potassium supplements or potassium-based salt substitutes: advise against use. A prescribed potassium supplement may be intentional (e.g. documented hypokalaemia) but needs a clear indication and monitoring.
management.monitoring: Serum potassium if a potassium supplement is intentionally continued with RAAS blockade.
management.patient_counselling: Avoid potassium-based salt substitutes ('low-sodium'/'heart' salts) and OTC potassium supplements unless the prescriber has specifically advised them.
management.exceptions: Prescribed potassium replacement for a genuine deficit is a confirm-and-monitor situation, not a counsel-to-avoid one.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — paraphrase: potassium supplements and potassium-containing salt substitutes may lead to hyperkalaemia with ACE inhibitors>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Potassium supplements or potassium-containing salt substitutes increase hyperkalaemia risk with ACE inhibitors/ARBs.

management_override.prescriber_action: Potassium supplementation with RAAS blockade at eGFR <30 is high-risk; clarify before supply.

mechanism: Reduced glomerular filtration and hyperkalaemia: NSAID blocks prostaglandin-mediated afferent vasodilation while ACEi/ARB reduce efferent tone; risk rises with volume depletion, older age and CKD.

management.prescriber_action: Prefer paracetamol for short-term analgesia; if an NSAID is intended, use lowest dose/shortest course, ensure hydration and arrange renal/potassium review — not a blanket ban.
management.monitoring: Check eGFR/creatinine and potassium if the NSAID is continued, especially in older or volume-depleted patients.
management.patient_counselling: Maintain hydration; stop the NSAID and seek review if reduced urine output, swelling or breathlessness.
management.exceptions: Add a diuretic and this becomes the higher-risk 'triple whammy' (see acei_arb_diuretic__nsaid_triple_whammy).

evidence.excerpt: <verify — paraphrase: NSAIDs may reduce the effect of and increase renal risk with ACE inhibitors/ARBs, particularly in volume-depleted or renally-impaired patients>
evidence.normalized_proposition: NSAIDs combined with ACE inhibitors/ARBs increase the risk of renal impairment and reduce antihypertensive effect.

management_override.prescriber_action: Avoid systemic NSAID where feasible; if essential, prescriber to arrange close renal/potassium monitoring.
Systemic NSAID generally contraindicated at eGFR <30 with RAAS blockade.

mechanism: 'Triple whammy' acute kidney injury: ACEi/ARB + diuretic + NSAID together impair renal autoregulation and volume status, a classic preventable-AKI trigger.

management.prescriber_action: Do not hand over the added systemic NSAID (usually the new or OTC item) to a patient established on ACEi/ARB + diuretic; clarify and prefer paracetamol. If an NSAID is genuinely required, prescriber to authorise the shortest course, ensure hydration and arrange a renal/potassium check. Do not stop the established ACEi/ARB or diuretic at the pharmacy.
management.monitoring: Baseline and short-interval eGFR/creatinine and potassium if the NSAID proceeds.
management.patient_counselling: Maintain fluids; hold the NSAID and seek urgent review with reduced urine output, swelling, vomiting/diarrhoea or breathlessness ('sick-day' guidance).
management.exceptions: Rule fires only when all three (ACEi/ARB + diuretic + NSAID) are co-present; the two-drug ACEi/ARB + NSAID case is the lower-tier acei_arb__nsaid_systemic. The withheld/clarified item is the added NSAID, never the established ACEi/ARB or diuretic.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — paraphrase: concurrent ACEi/ARB, diuretic and NSAID substantially increase acute kidney injury risk>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Concurrent ACEi/ARB, diuretic and NSAID ('triple whammy') substantially increase the risk of acute kidney injury.

management_override.prescriber_action: Do not add an NSAID to ACEi/ARB + diuretic at eGFR <30.

applicability.indication: dual RAAS blockade generally not recommended

mechanism: Dual renin-angiotensin system blockade increases hyperkalaemia, acute kidney injury and hypotension without net outcome benefit for most indications.

management.prescriber_action: Query whether dual ACEi+ARB is intended; guidelines discourage it for most indications. Do not unilaterally stop either agent — flag for prescriber review of the regimen.
management.monitoring: Potassium, eGFR/creatinine and blood pressure if the combination is continued.
management.patient_counselling: Report dizziness on standing, reduced urine output or palpitations.
management.exceptions: Rare specialist scenarios exist; the pharmacist escalates rather than discontinues.

management_override.prescriber_action: Dual RAAS blockade at eGFR <30 is high-risk; clarify urgently before supply.

mechanism: Trimethoprim blocks the distal epithelial sodium channel (amiloride-like), reducing potassium excretion; additive with other potassium-raising drugs. management.prescriber_action: Prefer an antibiotic without the potassium effect where clinically appropriate, especially in older patients, renal impairment, or when the background drug is spironolactone/eplerenone. If trimethoprim/co-trimoxazole is required, check baseline and on-treatment potassium.
management.monitoring: Serum potassium (and renal function) during therapy, particularly days 3-5, in older or renally-impaired patients and those on an MRA.
management.patient_counselling: Complete only the intended short antibiotic course; report palpitations or marked weakness.
management.exceptions: For the spironolactone/eplerenone + trimethoprim/co-trimoxazole high-risk pair in an older or renally-impaired patient, prefer withhold_and_clarify and an alternative antibiotic.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — paraphrase: hyperkalaemia reported, risk increased with other potassium-raising agents and in renal impairment>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Trimethoprim/co-trimoxazole causes hyperkalaemia and adds to the effect of other potassium-raising drugs.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — paraphrase: spironolactone plus trimethoprim/co-trimoxazole associated with hyperkalaemia and excess sudden death in older adults>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Spironolactone with trimethoprim/co-trimoxazole is associated with severe hyperkalaemia and increased sudden-death risk in older adults.

management_override.prescriber_action: At eGFR <30 with a potassium-raising drug, prefer an alternative antibiotic; clarify before supply.

mechanism: NSAIDs reduce renal lithium clearance (prostaglandin-mediated), raising lithium concentrations toward toxicity; effect occurs even at normal baseline renal function.

management.prescriber_action: Prefer paracetamol; if an NSAID is genuinely required alongside lithium, prescriber to check lithium level after starting AND after stopping and adjust dose. Do not stop lithium at the pharmacy.
management.monitoring: Lithium level ~5-7 days after starting or stopping the NSAID; renal function.
management.patient_counselling: Watch for lithium toxicity (tremor, vomiting, diarrhoea, drowsiness, unsteadiness); avoid OTC NSAIDs.
management.exceptions: Withhold applies to the NSAID (the new/OTC item), not to established lithium therapy.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — paraphrase: NSAIDs can reduce lithium clearance and increase lithium levels>
evidence.normalized_proposition: NSAIDs reduce lithium clearance and increase the risk of lithium toxicity.

management_override.prescriber_action: Avoid systemic NSAID with lithium in renal impairment; if unavoidable, intensive lithium-level and renal monitoring.

mechanism: ACE inhibitors/ARBs reduce renal lithium clearance (sodium/volume-mediated), raising lithium levels; risk greatest on initiation, dose change, dehydration or intercurrent illness.

management.prescriber_action: Both drugs are often intentionally co-prescribed; do not stop either at the pharmacy. Prescriber to check lithium level after any RAAS start/dose change and during dehydrating illness, adjusting lithium dose as needed.
management.monitoring: Lithium level ~1 week after RAAS initiation/dose change, then periodically; renal function and sodium.
management.patient_counselling: Stay hydrated; report vomiting/diarrhoea; watch for tremor, drowsiness, unsteadiness.
management.exceptions: 'Sick-day' dehydration sharply increases risk and warrants earlier level checks.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — paraphrase: ACE inhibitors/ARBs can increase serum lithium levels>
evidence.normalized_proposition: ACE inhibitors and ARBs increase serum lithium concentrations.

management_override.prescriber_action: Renal impairment increases lithium accumulation; closer level and renal monitoring.

mechanism: Thiazides cause sodium depletion and increased proximal lithium reabsorption, raising lithium levels (reported up to ~40%).

management.prescriber_action: If co-prescription is intended, prescriber to reduce lithium dose and check level after starting/stopping the thiazide. Do not stop lithium at the pharmacy.
management.monitoring: Lithium level ~5-7 days after thiazide start/stop or dose change; renal function and sodium.
management.patient_counselling: Report tremor, vomiting, diarrhoea, drowsiness or unsteadiness; maintain steady salt/fluid intake.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — paraphrase: thiazide diuretics reduce lithium clearance and raise lithium levels>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Thiazide diuretics increase serum lithium concentrations.

management_override.prescriber_action: Renal impairment compounds accumulation; closer monitoring and dose review.

mechanism: Additive oto- and nephrotoxicity; loop diuretics may also potentiate aminoglycoside ototoxicity via volume depletion and cochlear effects.

management.prescriber_action: Usually specialist/inpatient; ensure hydration, use lowest effective aminoglycoside course, therapeutic drug monitoring and renal/auditory surveillance. Do not unilaterally alter specialist therapy.
management.monitoring: Aminoglycoside levels, renal function (creatinine/eGFR) and clinical hearing/balance during therapy.
management.patient_counselling: Report hearing change, ringing in the ears, dizziness or reduced urine output.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — paraphrase: concurrent potent diuretics may increase aminoglycoside oto/nephrotoxicity>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Concurrent loop (potent) diuretics increase aminoglycoside oto- and nephrotoxicity.

management_override.prescriber_action: Renal impairment requires aminoglycoside dose/interval adjustment by levels and intensified monitoring.

mechanism: NSAIDs reduce renal methotrexate clearance (competition for tubular secretion), raising exposure and marrow/GI/mucosal toxicity. Risk is greatest with high-dose MTX or accumulation; dose spacing does NOT reliably prevent impaired clearance.

management.prescriber_action: Low-dose weekly methotrexate with a stable, prescriber-supervised NSAID may continue with monitoring for marrow/GI toxicity; for high-dose methotrexate, avoid the NSAID around dosing.
management.monitoring: Full blood count, renal and liver function; MTX level where a high-dose protocol applies.
management.patient_counselling: Report mouth ulcers, sore throat, fever, unusual bruising/bleeding, breathlessness; confirm once-WEEKLY (never daily) MTX dosing.
management.exceptions: Reserve the higher tier for high-dose MTX or significant accumulation risk; a stable supervised low-dose-weekly + NSAID pairing is not automatically Major.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — paraphrase: NSAIDs may reduce methotrexate clearance and increase toxicity, particularly with high-dose regimens>
evidence.normalized_proposition: NSAIDs reduce methotrexate clearance and increase methotrexate toxicity, especially at high doses.

management_override.prescriber_action: Avoid systemic NSAID with MTX in renal impairment; reduced clearance risks marrow toxicity.
MTX with a systemic NSAID at eGFR <30 is high-risk for accumulation and pancytopenia; withhold and clarify.

mechanism: Additive antifolate effect (both inhibit folate pathways) plus reduced MTX renal clearance, risking severe bone-marrow suppression/pancytopenia even with low-dose weekly MTX.

management.prescriber_action: Generally avoid; prefer an alternative antibiotic. The withheld/clarified item is the newly-dispensed antibiotic, not established MTX. If genuinely unavoidable, specialist decision with intensive haematological monitoring and folinic-acid support.
management.monitoring: Full blood count during and after the course; renal and liver function.
management.patient_counselling: Report sore throat, fever, mouth ulcers, unusual bruising/bleeding; confirm once-WEEKLY MTX dosing.
management.exceptions: Applies to both low-dose weekly and high-dose MTX; co-trimoxazole/trimethoprim is a well-recognised avoid-combination with MTX.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — paraphrase: concomitant trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole may increase bone-marrow suppression with methotrexate>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Trimethoprim/co-trimoxazole with methotrexate increases the risk of bone-marrow suppression.

management_override.prescriber_action: At eGFR <30 the combination is especially dangerous; withhold and require an alternative antibiotic.

applicability.indication: scoped to HIGH-DOSE methotrexate (oncology protocol); not a general alert for low-dose weekly MTX

mechanism: PPIs may delay high-dose methotrexate elimination (impaired renal/tubular transport), prolonging toxic exposure and delaying clearance below safe thresholds.

management.prescriber_action: In high-dose MTX protocols, oncology may hold/switch the PPI (e.g. to an H2 antagonist) around the MTX cycle per protocol. Pharmacist confirms with the oncology team; does not unilaterally alter therapy.
management.monitoring: MTX levels and clearance, renal function during the high-dose cycle.
management.patient_counselling: Adhere to the oncology team's instructions on acid-suppression timing around chemotherapy.
management.exceptions: Low-dose weekly MTX + PPI is generally not clinically significant and is out of scope for this rule.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — paraphrase: PPIs may reduce elimination of high-dose methotrexate, increasing/prolonging levels>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Proton pump inhibitors may delay elimination of high-dose methotrexate and prolong toxic exposure.

management_override.prescriber_action: Delayed high-dose MTX clearance with renal impairment is dangerous; escalate to the oncology team before proceeding.

mechanism: Strong dual CYP3A4 and P-gp inhibition reduces colchicine elimination, causing accumulation and potentially fatal toxicity (myelosuppression, neuromyopathy, multi-organ failure).

management.prescriber_action: Withhold and clarify with the prescriber: colchicine with a strong CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitor risks serious or fatal colchicine toxicity. The prescriber must interrupt colchicine or reduce the dose per the specific inhibitor's label before the interacting drug is used.
management.monitoring: Watch for colchicine toxicity (diarrhoea, vomiting, myalgia, weakness, cytopenias); assess renal and hepatic function.
management.patient_counselling: Stop colchicine and seek urgent care for muscle pain or weakness, numbness, persistent vomiting or diarrhoea, unusual bruising, or signs of infection.
management.exceptions: Some labels permit a reduced-dose course or a treatment interruption when renal and hepatic function are normal; confirm the specific inhibitor and colchicine indication with the prescriber.

evidence.excerpt: <verify - fatal toxicity reported with strong CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors; combination contraindicated in patients with renal or hepatic impairment>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Strong CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors raise colchicine exposure; the combination is contraindicated in renal or hepatic impairment and otherwise requires dose reduction or interruption.

management_override.prescriber_action: Contraindicated with a strong CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitor in renal impairment: do not co-supply; refer to prescriber.
Contraindicated with a strong CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitor in hepatic impairment: do not co-supply; refer to prescriber.

mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 inhibition (macrolides, azole antifungals, HIV protease inhibitors) raises ergot alkaloid concentrations, causing acute ergotism with peripheral and cerebral vasospasm and ischaemia.

management.prescriber_action: Combination is contraindicated: do not co-supply. Prescriber to select a non-interacting alternative for the migraine or uterotonic indication.
management.patient_counselling: Seek urgent care for cold, numb, or painful hands or feet, chest pain, or severe or unusual headache.

evidence.excerpt: <verify - coadministration with potent CYP3A4 inhibitors (protease inhibitors, macrolide antibiotics, azole antifungals) is contraindicated due to risk of acute ergot toxicity>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Potent CYP3A4 inhibitors are contraindicated with ergotamine because of the risk of acute ergot toxicity (ergotism).

mechanism: CYP3A4 (and CYP2D6) inhibition raises pimozide exposure, causing dose-dependent QT prolongation and potentially fatal arrhythmia.

management.prescriber_action: Label-contraindicated with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (and CYP2D6 inhibitors): do not co-supply. Prescriber to choose a non-interacting antimicrobial or an alternative antipsychotic.
management.patient_counselling: Seek care for palpitations, fainting, or dizziness.
management.exceptions: Applies to label-listed strong and selected inhibitors. Additive QT risk from co-prescribed QT-prolonging drugs is a separate additive-QT assessment, not this contraindication.

evidence.excerpt: <verify - contraindicated with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors including macrolide antibiotics and azole antifungals owing to QT prolongation and arrhythmia risk>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors are contraindicated with pimozide due to QT prolongation and arrhythmia risk.

mechanism: CYP3A4 inhibition (azole antifungals, macrolides, diltiazem and others) reduces tacrolimus metabolism, raising exposure and risk of nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity, and over-immunosuppression.

management.prescriber_action: Do not stop tacrolimus. The transplant team should reduce the dose and arrange early and frequent trough-level monitoring before and after the inhibitor is started or stopped.
management.monitoring: Tacrolimus trough levels, renal function, and toxicity; check on starting and on stopping the inhibitor.
management.patient_counselling: Do not stop your transplant medicine; report tremor, headache, reduced urine output, or new symptoms; avoid grapefruit.
management.exceptions: Grapefruit and grapefruit juice also inhibit gut CYP3A4 and should be avoided (see grapefruit rule).

evidence.excerpt: <verify - CYP3A4 inhibitors increase tacrolimus whole-blood concentrations; monitor levels and adjust dose>
evidence.normalized_proposition: CYP3A4 inhibitors raise tacrolimus exposure and require dose reduction with trough-level monitoring.

management_override.monitoring: Hepatic impairment further reduces tacrolimus clearance; monitor trough levels more frequently.

mechanism: CYP3A4 and P-gp inhibition reduces ciclosporin metabolism and transport, raising exposure and risk of nephrotoxicity, hypertension, and neurotoxicity.

management.prescriber_action: Do not stop ciclosporin. Specialist to dose-adjust guided by trough levels with renal-function monitoring.
management.monitoring: Ciclosporin trough levels, renal function, blood pressure.
management.patient_counselling: Do not stop your transplant medicine; avoid grapefruit; report reduced urine output or swelling.
management.exceptions: Grapefruit and grapefruit juice also inhibit gut CYP3A4 and should be avoided (see grapefruit rule).

evidence.excerpt: <verify - CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors increase cyclosporine concentrations; monitor levels and renal function>
evidence.normalized_proposition: CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors raise ciclosporin exposure and require dose adjustment with level and renal monitoring.

management_override.monitoring: Hepatic impairment reduces ciclosporin clearance; monitor trough levels more frequently.

mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 and P-gp inhibition markedly raises sirolimus exposure, increasing risk of immunosuppression-related and dose-related toxicity.

management.prescriber_action: Concomitant strong CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors (for example ketoconazole, voriconazole, clarithromycin) are not recommended with sirolimus: do not add without a transplant-team decision. If an interacting drug is essential, dose-adjust with trough monitoring. Do not stop sirolimus.
management.monitoring: Sirolimus trough levels, renal and hepatic function, lipids, blood counts.
management.patient_counselling: Do not stop your transplant medicine; avoid grapefruit; report new symptoms.
management.exceptions: Moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors are used with caution plus level monitoring rather than avoidance.

evidence.excerpt: <verify - concomitant use with strong CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors is not recommended; strong inhibitors markedly increase sirolimus concentrations>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Strong CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors are not recommended with sirolimus because they markedly raise sirolimus exposure.

management_override.monitoring: Hepatic impairment reduces sirolimus clearance; monitor trough levels more frequently.

mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 induction (rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine) accelerates tacrolimus and ciclosporin metabolism, lowering levels to subtherapeutic and risking graft rejection.

management.prescriber_action: Do not stop the immunosuppressant. Transplant team to increase the dose guided by trough levels, or select a non-inducing alternative to the inducer, and re-adjust when the inducer is stopped.
management.monitoring: Immunosuppressant trough levels and graft function on starting and on stopping the inducer.
management.patient_counselling: Do not stop your transplant medicine; report symptoms of rejection; do not start St John's Wort.

evidence.excerpt: <verify - CYP3A4 inducers decrease tacrolimus and ciclosporin concentrations; monitor levels and adjust dose>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Strong CYP3A4 inducers lower tacrolimus and ciclosporin exposure and require dose increase with trough monitoring to avoid rejection.

mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 inhibition raises sildenafil exposure, increasing risk of hypotension, visual disturbance, and syncope.

management.prescriber_action: Concomitant potent CYP3A4 inhibitors (for example ritonavir, ketoconazole, itraconazole) with sildenafil for PAH are not recommended; PAH specialist to review before co-starting.
management.monitoring: Blood pressure and symptoms of hypotension.
management.patient_counselling: Report dizziness, fainting, or vision changes.
management.exceptions: Sildenafil for erectile dysfunction uses a dose-reduction approach (for example 25 mg) with strong inhibitors and is handled as a separate rule.

evidence.excerpt: <verify - concomitant use of Revatio with potent CYP3A4 inhibitors such as ritonavir is not recommended>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Potent CYP3A4 inhibitors are not recommended with sildenafil used for pulmonary arterial hypertension.

management_override.monitoring: Hepatic impairment raises sildenafil exposure; monitor blood pressure more closely.

mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 inhibition raises tadalafil exposure, increasing risk of hypotension and other dose-related effects.

management.prescriber_action: For tadalafil in PAH with a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor, follow label-specific dosing (initiation and dose restrictions vary by inhibitor); PAH specialist to review before co-starting.
management.monitoring: Blood pressure and symptoms of hypotension.
management.patient_counselling: Report dizziness, fainting, or prolonged headache.
management.exceptions: Tadalafil for erectile dysfunction or benign prostatic hyperplasia has separate dose limits with strong inhibitors and is handled as a separate rule.

mechanism: Rifamycins are potent CYP3A4 (plus UGT and P-gp) inducers that accelerate metabolism of contraceptive oestrogen and progestogen, lowering plasma levels and risking contraceptive failure and unintended pregnancy.

management.duration: Effect persists throughout rifamycin therapy and about 28 days after the last dose as enzyme activity recovers.
management.exceptions: Depot medroxyprogesterone (DMPA) injection and intrauterine methods (copper IUD, levonorgestrel IUS) are NOT clinically affected and are the preferred alternatives; do not extend this rule to non-hormonal methods.

management.duration: For the whole antibiotic course.
management.exceptions: Chelation applies to oral tetracyclines only.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — absorption of tetracyclines reduced by antacids, iron and other polyvalent cations; separate administration>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Polyvalent cations reduce oral doxycycline absorption; separate administration.

mechanism: Calcium, iron and other polyvalent-cation binders bind levothyroxine in the gut and reduce its absorption, risking under-treatment (raised TSH).

management.monitoring: Recheck TSH if consistent separation cannot be maintained.
management.patient_counselling: Take levothyroxine on an empty stomach and separate it from calcium, iron and antacids.
management.timing: Separate levothyroxine from cation binders by at least 4 hours.
management.duration: For as long as both are taken.
management.exceptions: This binder rule is resolved by clock-spacing; the pH-modifier (PPI) interaction is a SEPARATE rule not solved by spacing.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — calcium/iron/antacids reduce levothyroxine absorption; separate by at least 4 h>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Oral cation binders reduce levothyroxine absorption; separate dosing by at least 4 hours.

mechanism: Sustained reduction of gastric acidity impairs dissolution and absorption of levothyroxine (esp. tablets), lowering levels and raising TSH; unlike binders, this is NOT overcome by clock-spacing.

management.prescriber_action: Recheck TSH after starting, stopping or changing acid-suppressant therapy; the levothyroxine dose may need adjustment. Do not stop either drug at the counter.
management.monitoring: TSH about 4-8 weeks after any change in acid-suppressant therapy.
management.patient_counselling: Take levothyroxine the same way every day; tell your prescriber if you start or stop indigestion/heartburn medicines.
management.duration: For as long as the acid suppressant is used.
management.exceptions: Clock-spacing does NOT overcome continuous PPI acid suppression — manage by consistent administration plus TSH review, not separation alone.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — agents that reduce gastric acidity may decrease levothyroxine absorption; monitor TSH>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Acid suppressants can reduce levothyroxine absorption; monitor TSH after changes rather than relying on dose separation.

mechanism: Oral bisphosphonate bioavailability is very low and is abolished by food, coffee, juice, mineral water and polyvalent cations taken at the same time.

management.patient_counselling: Take alendronate first thing in the morning on an empty stomach with a full glass of PLAIN water only; wait at least 30 minutes before any food, drink, other medicine or supplement; remain upright (sitting or standing) during that time.
management.timing: At least 30 minutes before the first food, drink, medicine or cation of the day; plain water only.
management.duration: Every dose.
management.exceptions: Product-specific to alendronate — do NOT copy the 30-minute/plain-water rule to other bisphosphonates or delayed-release formulations without checking their own label.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — take on arising for the day with plain water, at least 30 min before first food/beverage/medication, remain upright>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Alendronate must be taken on an empty stomach with plain water, at least 30 minutes before any food, drink, other medicine or cation, staying upright.

mechanism: Oral risedronate absorption is reduced by food and polyvalent cations; the correct administration differs between the immediate-release and delayed-release products.

management.patient_counselling: Immediate-release risedronate: take on an empty stomach with plain water, at least 30 minutes before the first food/drink/medicine, stay upright. Delayed-release risedronate: take immediately AFTER breakfast with at least 4 oz of plain water, stay upright — do not apply the empty-stomach rule.
management.timing: Immediate-release: >=30 minutes before first food/drink/medicine, plain water, upright. Delayed-release: immediately after breakfast per its own label.
management.duration: Every dose.
management.exceptions: Formulation-specific: delayed-release risedronate is taken WITH food and must not be managed like the immediate-release tablet; separate calcium/iron/antacid supplements from either formulation.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — immediate-release taken >=30 min before first food; delayed-release taken immediately after breakfast>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Risedronate administration is formulation-specific: immediate-release before food on an empty stomach; delayed-release after breakfast.

mechanism: Oral ibandronate bioavailability is abolished by food and polyvalent cations; it requires a LONGER pre-food fast than alendronate/risedronate immediate-release.

management.patient_counselling: Take oral ibandronate first thing in the morning on an empty stomach with a full glass of plain water only; wait at least 60 minutes before any food, drink, other medicine or supplement; stay upright during that time.
management.timing: At least 60 minutes before the first food, drink, medicine or cation of the day; plain water only.
management.duration: Every dose (typically once monthly).
management.exceptions: Product-specific 60-minute interval — do not substitute alendronate's 30-minute rule.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — take with plain water at least 60 min before first food/drink/medication, remain upright>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Oral ibandronate must be taken on an empty stomach with plain water at least 60 minutes before any food, drink, medicine or cation.

mechanism: Raising gastric pH reduces atazanavir solubility and absorption, producing subtherapeutic levels with risk of virologic failure and resistance; magnitude depends on the booster and treatment history.

management.prescriber_action: Confirm the regimen with the HIV prescriber before supplying the acid suppressant: boosted atazanavir has PPI dose caps and separation requirements, and PPIs are not recommended in treatment-experienced patients. Do NOT stop antiretroviral therapy.
management.monitoring: HIV viral load if an acid suppressant is used.
management.patient_counselling: Do not start over-the-counter antacids, H2 blockers or PPIs without telling your HIV clinic; the dose and timing matter.
management.timing: Where permitted: give boosted atazanavir and the PPI at least 12 hours apart with the PPI dose capped; separate antacids/buffered products by at least 2 hours; H2-antagonist limits and separation per label.
management.duration: Whole period of overlap.
management.exceptions: Severity and permissibility vary by booster (ritonavir/cobicistat) and by treatment-naive vs treatment-experienced status — split from unboosted atazanavir at promotion if needed.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — acid-reducing agents decrease atazanavir exposure; PPI dose/timing restrictions; not recommended in treatment-experienced patients>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Acid suppressants reduce atazanavir exposure; use is restricted by booster and treatment history with dose caps and separation requirements.

mechanism: PPIs cause sustained gastric pH elevation that substantially reduces rilpivirine absorption, risking loss of virologic response and resistance; the label lists PPIs as contraindicated with rilpivirine.

management.prescriber_action: PPIs are contraindicated with rilpivirine — do not supply the PPI alongside rilpivirine; contact the HIV prescriber for an alternative acid-reducing strategy. Do NOT stop antiretroviral therapy.
management.patient_counselling: Do not take proton-pump-inhibitor heartburn medicines (e.g. omeprazole, esomeprazole) while on rilpivirine.
management.exceptions: H2-antagonists may be used only with strict separation (e.g. taken >=12 h before or >=4 h after rilpivirine); antacids taken >=2 h before or >=4 h after rilpivirine — these are the timed alternatives, distinct from the contraindicated PPIs. Verify against current label.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — proton pump inhibitors are contraindicated with rilpivirine due to reduced rilpivirine exposure>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Proton pump inhibitors are contraindicated with rilpivirine; H2-antagonists and antacids are permitted only with strict dose separation.

mechanism: Erlotinib solubility is pH-dependent; acid suppression lowers erlotinib exposure and may reduce anti-tumour efficacy. Sustained PPI suppression is NOT overcome by dose separation.

management.prescriber_action: Avoid PPIs where possible; clarify the acid-reducing plan with oncology. Do NOT stop the tyrosine-kinase inhibitor at the counter.
management.patient_counselling: Tell your cancer team before using any antacid, H2 blocker or heartburn medicine.
management.timing: PPIs: avoid (spacing does not help). Antacids: separate by several hours. H2-antagonist: take erlotinib about 10 hours after and at least 2 hours before the H2 dose (per label).
management.duration: Whole period of overlap.
management.exceptions: Spacing overcomes antacids but NOT continuous PPI suppression; member-specific timing.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — concomitant acid-reducing agents decrease erlotinib exposure; avoid PPIs; antacid/H2 timing guidance>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Acid suppressants reduce erlotinib exposure; avoid PPIs and apply labelled timing for antacids/H2-antagonists.

management_override.prescriber_action: Hepatic impairment independently raises erlotinib exposure and toxicity risk; oncology should factor this into the acid-suppressant decision and any dose review.

mechanism: Dasatinib solubility is pH-dependent; PPIs and H2-antagonists markedly reduce dasatinib exposure and may reduce efficacy. Spacing does not overcome sustained suppression.

management.prescriber_action: PPIs and H2-antagonists are not recommended with dasatinib; if acid reduction is needed, antacids may be used with separation. Clarify with oncology; do NOT stop the TKI at the counter.
management.patient_counselling: Do not use PPIs or H2 blockers with dasatinib without oncology advice; if an antacid is needed, keep it well apart from the dose.
management.timing: Antacids: give at least 2 hours before or at least 2 hours after dasatinib. Avoid concurrent PPI or H2-antagonist.
management.duration: Whole period of overlap.
management.exceptions: Antacid separation is acceptable; PPI/H2 suppression is not solved by timing.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — avoid concomitant PPIs and H2-antagonists; antacids may be given >=2 h before or after dasatinib>
evidence.normalized_proposition: PPIs/H2-antagonists reduce dasatinib exposure and should be avoided; antacids are permitted only with 2-hour separation.

management_override.prescriber_action: Hepatic impairment affects dasatinib handling; oncology should factor this into the acid-suppressant decision and any dose review.

mechanism: Oral ketoconazole tablets require gastric acid to dissolve and be absorbed; reduced acidity lowers absorption and antifungal efficacy.

management.prescriber_action: If acid reduction is unavoidable, the ketoconazole tablet should be taken with an acidic beverage and the antifungal response reviewed; clarify with the prescriber. Do not stop specialist antifungal therapy at the counter.
management.monitoring: Watch for lack of antifungal response.
management.patient_counselling: If you must take an acid-reducing medicine, take ketoconazole tablets with an acidic drink (e.g. a non-diet cola) and keep antacids well separated.
management.timing: Antacids/H2: separate by at least 2 hours. PPIs cause sustained acid suppression not solved by spacing — clarify with prescriber.
management.duration: Whole period of overlap.
management.exceptions: The acidic-beverage advice is product-specific to ketoconazole TABLETS and must NOT be generalised to other azoles or formulations.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — drugs that reduce gastric acidity impair ketoconazole absorption; take with acidic beverage when acid reducers required>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Acid suppressants reduce oral ketoconazole absorption; where unavoidable, take the tablet with an acidic beverage and separate antacids.

management_override.prescriber_action: Oral ketoconazole is hepatotoxic and hepatically cleared; in hepatic impairment the prescriber should reconsider the antifungal choice rather than simply adding an acidic drink.

mechanism: Itraconazole CAPSULE absorption requires an acidic gastric environment; acid suppression markedly reduces absorption and antifungal efficacy.

management.prescriber_action: If acid reduction is unavoidable, itraconazole capsules should be taken with food and an acidic beverage, and the response reviewed; clarify with the prescriber. Consider whether a formulation whose absorption is not acid-dependent is more appropriate. Do not stop specialist antifungal therapy at the counter.
management.monitoring: Watch for lack of antifungal response.
management.patient_counselling: Take itraconazole capsules with food and an acidic drink (e.g. a non-diet cola) if you need an acid-reducing medicine; keep antacids well separated.
management.timing: Antacids: separate by at least 1-2 hours. PPIs cause sustained suppression not solved by spacing — clarify with prescriber.
management.duration: Whole period of overlap.
management.exceptions: Applies to the CAPSULE formulation only; do NOT apply the acidic-drink advice to itraconazole oral solution (separate rule).

evidence.excerpt: <verify — reduced gastric acidity decreases absorption of itraconazole capsules; take with food/acidic beverage>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Acid suppressants reduce itraconazole CAPSULE absorption; take with food and an acidic beverage and separate antacids.

management_override.prescriber_action: Itraconazole is hepatotoxic and hepatically cleared (and a negative inotrope); in hepatic impairment the prescriber should review antifungal appropriateness, not simply adjust administration.

mechanism: Fluconazole inhibits CYP2C9, reducing clearance of CYP2C9-metabolised sulfonylureas (glipizide, glimepiride, glibenclamide, tolbutamide) so exposure rises and hypoglycaemia is prolonged.

management.prescriber_action: Confirm the antifungal is intended alongside the sulfonylurea; consider a lower sulfonylurea dose for the antifungal course or a non-interacting antifungal.
management.monitoring: Advise more frequent blood-glucose self-monitoring during and shortly after the fluconazole course.
management.patient_counselling: Recognise and treat hypoglycaemia (sweating, tremor, confusion, hunger); carry fast-acting glucose.
management.duration: Interaction persists for the fluconazole course plus a few days after (enzyme recovery).
management.exceptions: Single-dose 150 mg oral fluconazole (as used for vaginal candidiasis) has a smaller effect than multi-day systemic courses; gliclazide is less CYP2C9-dependent than glimepiride/glipizide.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — fluconazole raises sulfonylurea exposure and hypoglycaemia risk>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Fluconazole increases plasma concentrations of CYP2C9-metabolised sulfonylureas and can cause hypoglycaemia.

management_override.prescriber_action: Renal impairment prolongs sulfonylurea and metabolite exposure; withhold and clarify dose or agent choice before supply.

mechanism: Sulfamethoxazole inhibits CYP2C9 and displaces sulfonylureas from protein binding, raising free sulfonylurea concentrations and causing marked, sometimes prolonged, hypoglycaemia.

management.prescriber_action: Confirm the antibiotic is intended alongside the sulfonylurea; consider a lower sulfonylurea dose for the course or a non-interacting antibacterial.
management.monitoring: Advise more frequent blood-glucose self-monitoring during and shortly after the co-trimoxazole course.
management.patient_counselling: Recognise and treat hypoglycaemia; carry fast-acting glucose.
management.duration: Applies for the antibiotic course plus a short period afterwards.
management.exceptions: Effect magnitude varies by sulfonylurea member; elderly and renally impaired patients are more affected.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — co-trimoxazole can potentiate sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Co-trimoxazole can potentiate the hypoglycaemic effect of sulfonylureas.

management_override.prescriber_action: Renal impairment prolongs sulfonylurea exposure and adds hyperkalaemia risk from co-trimoxazole; withhold and clarify before supply.

mechanism: Gemfibrozil inhibits CYP2C8/2C9 and can modestly raise exposure to some sulfonylureas, adding to hypoglycaemia risk; the effect is not uniform across the class (largest for meglitinides, variable for individual sulfonylureas).

management.prescriber_action: Where a fibrate is needed, review whether a non-gemfibrozil fibrate is more appropriate; monitor glycaemic control.
management.monitoring: Blood-glucose monitoring, particularly when either drug is started or dose-changed.
management.patient_counselling: Recognise and treat hypoglycaemia.
management.duration: For the duration of overlap.
management.exceptions: Effect is member-specific and generally modest for sulfonylureas; do not expand mechanically to the whole class at equal severity.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — gemfibrozil may enhance the hypoglycaemic effect of sulfonylureas>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Gemfibrozil may enhance the hypoglycaemic effect of some sulfonylureas.

mechanism: Alcohol impairs hepatic gluconeogenesis and masks warning signs, potentiating and prolonging sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia (a pharmacodynamic effect, not simply CYP2C9 inhibition); chlorpropamide and some others can also produce a disulfiram-like flushing reaction with alcohol.

management.prescriber_action: No routine dose change; reinforce alcohol-and-hypoglycaemia counselling at review.
management.monitoring: Blood-glucose awareness around alcohol intake, especially fasting or binge drinking.
management.patient_counselling: Avoid drinking on an empty stomach; alcohol can cause delayed, severe hypoglycaemia; a flushing reaction may occur with chlorpropamide-type agents.
management.exceptions: Disulfiram-like reaction is member-specific (notably chlorpropamide); the hypoglycaemia risk is a class effect.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — alcohol may provoke hypoglycaemia and a disulfiram-like reaction with sulfonylureas>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Alcohol can potentiate sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia and, with some agents, cause a disulfiram-like reaction.

mechanism: Miconazole is a potent CYP2C9 inhibitor and the oromucosal gel is absorbed systemically enough to markedly raise sulfonylurea exposure, causing severe hypoglycaemia; some jurisdictions label this combination as contraindicated.

management.prescriber_action: Under UK/EU labelling this pairing is contraindicated for selected sulfonylureas; withhold the gel and clarify an alternative antifungal (e.g. non-azole/topical strategy) with the prescriber.
management.monitoring: If the combination is nonetheless prescriber-directed, intensive blood-glucose monitoring is required.
management.patient_counselling: Do not use miconazole oral gel with your diabetes tablet without the prescriber's specific instruction; watch for hypoglycaemia.
management.duration: For the whole period of overlap.
management.exceptions: Topical skin miconazole (minimal systemic absorption) is not covered by this rule; US labelling treats the interaction as a warning rather than an absolute contraindication (jurisdiction to verify).

evidence.excerpt: <verify — miconazole oromucosal gel contraindicated with certain sulfonylureas due to hypoglycaemia>
evidence.normalized_proposition: In UK/EU labelling, miconazole oromucosal gel is contraindicated with selected sulfonylureas because of severe hypoglycaemia risk.

mechanism: Iodinated contrast can precipitate acute kidney injury; if renal function falls, metformin accumulates and raises the risk of lactic acidosis. Metformin does not itself interact pharmacokinetically with contrast.

management.prescriber_action: Metformin need not be stopped for all contrast. Follow imaging protocol: interrupt around the procedure for specified renal/clinical-risk groups and for intra-arterial contrast; reassess renal function ~48 h post-contrast and restart when stable.
management.monitoring: Recheck renal function ~48 h after contrast before restarting metformin in at-risk patients.
management.patient_counselling: Tell the imaging/procedure team you take metformin and follow their hold-and-restart instructions.
management.timing: Peri-procedural hold where indicated, not routine long-term spacing.
management.duration: Withhold from the time of contrast until renal function is confirmed stable (~48 h).
management.exceptions: Routine low-osmolar intravenous contrast in patients with normal renal function generally does not require interruption.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — discontinue metformin at time of iodinated contrast in at-risk patients; reassess renal function and restart>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Metformin should be interrupted around iodinated contrast in specified at-risk groups and restarted once renal function is confirmed stable.

management_override.prescriber_action: eGFR <30: metformin is contraindicated; do not co-administer around contrast — clarify the hold and interim glycaemic control.
eGFR 30-60 or intra-arterial contrast: interrupt metformin at the time of contrast and recheck renal function ~48 h before restart.

review.clinician_flag: on_unknown changed escalate->base: unknown renal -> base 'major/hold peri-procedure' rather than 'contraindicated' (contra needs eGFR<30). Confirm policy.

mechanism: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, the main inactivation route for azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine, shunting metabolism toward active thioguanine nucleotides and causing severe myelosuppression.

management.prescriber_action: Do not add the second agent without a plan: reduce the thiopurine to about 25% of the usual dose (roughly a 75% reduction) with regular FBC monitoring, or choose an alternative urate-lowering strategy. Do not unilaterally stop specialist-initiated thiopurine therapy.
management.monitoring: Full blood count (and thiopurine metabolites where available) at baseline and regularly after any change.
management.patient_counselling: Report fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, unusual bruising or bleeding, or infections.
management.duration: Applies for the whole period of overlap.
management.exceptions: TPMT/NUDT15-deficient patients are at even higher risk; febuxostat (a stronger xanthine oxidase inhibitor) with a thiopurine is a separate, generally contraindicated pairing.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — reduce thiopurine dose to about one-quarter when given with allopurinol>
evidence.normalized_proposition: When allopurinol is given with azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine, the thiopurine dose must be reduced to roughly one-quarter to avoid severe myelosuppression.

management_override.prescriber_action: Renal impairment raises allopurinol/oxypurinol and thiopurine metabolite exposure; withhold and clarify a reduced-dose plan with FBC monitoring before supply.

mechanism: CYP1A2 inhibitors (ciprofloxacin, fluvoxamine, cimetidine) reduce theophylline clearance, raising levels of this narrow-therapeutic-index drug and causing nausea, tachyarrhythmia and seizures.

management.prescriber_action: Prefer a non-interacting alternative (e.g. an antibiotic that does not inhibit CYP1A2). If the inhibitor is needed, reduce the theophylline dose (often by about half for strong inhibitors) and check a theophylline level.
management.monitoring: Serum theophylline level after starting and after stopping the inhibitor; watch for toxicity.
management.patient_counselling: Report nausea, vomiting, palpitations, tremor, agitation or seizures — these can signal theophylline toxicity.
management.duration: Adjust for the inhibitor course; re-review the level when it stops.
management.exceptions: Inhibitor potency differs (ciprofloxacin/fluvoxamine strong; cimetidine moderate; levofloxacin/ofloxacin much weaker) — member-specific severity applies.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — CYP1A2 inhibitors reduce theophylline clearance and increase toxicity risk>
evidence.normalized_proposition: CYP1A2 inhibitors reduce theophylline clearance and increase the risk of theophylline toxicity.

management_override.prescriber_action: Hepatic impairment already lowers theophylline clearance; withhold and clarify a reduced dose with level monitoring before adding a CYP1A2 inhibitor.

mechanism: Anticholinergic/antimuscarinic agents and other drugs that markedly slow GI transit prolong passage of solid oral potassium chloride, extending local mucosal contact with concentrated potassium and risking GI ulceration, bleeding, stricture or perforation. This is a local formulation hazard, not systemic hyperkalaemia.

management.prescriber_action: For solid modified-release/wax-matrix KCl plus an agent that markedly delays GI transit, switch to a liquid/effervescent (dissolved) potassium formulation or reconsider the transit-slowing drug; 'take with food' does not remove the hazard.
management.monitoring: Ask about and report GI symptoms: abdominal pain, vomiting, GI bleeding.
management.patient_counselling: Report abdominal pain, black/bloody stools or vomiting; a switch to a dissolved potassium formulation is preferred over any solid tablet here.
management.exceptions: Liquid, effervescent or fully dissolved potassium preparations are not subject to this contraindication; weak/transient anticholinergic effect carries lower risk than sustained transit slowing (severity to be confirmed by the reviewing clinician: contraindicated vs major).

evidence.excerpt: <verify — solid oral KCl contraindicated where GI passage is delayed, including by concomitant anticholinergic agents>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Solid oral potassium chloride is contraindicated where there is a pharmacologic cause (e.g. anticholinergic agents) for delayed GI passage.
